H1.text: A doctor checks your temperature. A shopkeeper weighs rice. You measure a table.

H2.text: Three very different jobs. But all three use the same basic idea.

H3.text: Even Diya's recipe card needs it. It says: sugar, two.

H4.text: Two spoons? Two cups? Two kilograms? The number alone means nothing.

H5.text: By the end of this video, you will see why. It is the first big idea in physics.

P1.text: So what is a physical quantity?

P2.text: It is anything in nature that we can measure. Length, mass, time, temperature, speed.

P3.text: Kindness and beauty matter, but no instrument can measure them. So they are not physical quantities.

P4.text: Every measurement has two parts. A number, called the magnitude. And a unit.

P5.text: A unit is a fixed amount we all agree on, like one metre or one kilogram.

S1.text: Let's measure one pencil on our measuring bench.

S2.text: With a centimetre scale, it reads fifteen. Fifteen centimetres.

S3.text: Switch to millimetres. Now it reads one hundred and fifty.

S4.text: Switch to metres. Now it is only zero point one five.

S5.text: The pencil never changed. The number and the unit changed together.

S6.text: Look at the graph. Unit ten times bigger, number ten times smaller.

D1.text: Let's write this as a rule, one step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. A quantity Q equals its number n, times its unit u. Q equals n u.

D3.text: Step two. The same quantity in two different units does not change. So n one u one equals n two u two.

D4.text: Step three. n times u is fixed, so n is inversely proportional to u. A bigger unit means a smaller number.

T1.text: Remember this. A physical quantity is always a number with a unit, never a number alone.

C1.text: Now, physicists sort quantities in two big ways.

C2.text: The first way: base quantities and derived quantities.

C3.text: Base quantities are the building blocks. The SI system picks seven of them.

C4.text: Length, mass, time, electric current, temperature, amount of substance, and luminous intensity.

R1.text: Derived quantities are built from these. Take speed.

R2.text: Speed equals distance divided by time.

R3.text: Distance is a length, so it is a base quantity. Time is also a base quantity.

R4.text: So speed is made from two base quantities. That is why speed is derived.

K1.text: Side by side. Length is base. You read it straight off a ruler.

K2.text: Speed is derived. You need a length and a time, and then you divide.

K3.text: Now you try. Is temperature a base quantity or a derived quantity? Pause the video and decide.

K4.text: Base! Temperature is one of the seven. A thermometer reads it directly, and it is not built from length, mass or time.

V1.text: The second way: scalars and vectors.

V2.text: A scalar has only a size. Five kilograms of rice is just five kilograms. No direction needed.

V3.text: A vector has a size and a direction. Displacement, velocity and force are vectors.

V4.text: Push a box with ten newtons to the right. It moves right.

V5.text: Push with the same ten newtons to the left, and it moves left. Same size, different result. So force needs a direction.

V6.text: Your turn. Is velocity a scalar or a vector? Pause and decide.

V7.text: A vector! Velocity is speed in a given direction. Fifty kilometres per hour north is not the same as fifty south.

G1.text: Let's sort six quantities on the board.

G2.text: Mass and time are base, and scalar.

G3.text: Speed and density are derived, and scalar.

G4.text: Velocity and force are derived, and they are vectors.

G5.text: Notice one box stays empty. None of the seven base quantities is a vector.

W2.text: A steel rod is two point five metres long. How long is it in centimetres?

W3.text: Use the rule. n two equals n one times u one, divided by u two.

W4.text: Here n one is two point five. u one is one metre. u two is one centimetre.

W5.text: One metre is one hundred centimetres. So n two is two point five times one hundred.

W6.text: That is two hundred and fifty. The rod is two hundred and fifty centimetres long.

X2.text: Many students say electric current is a vector, because it flows in a direction.

X3.text: But current is a scalar. At a junction, two amperes and three amperes always make five amperes, whatever the angle. Vectors do not add like that.

E1.text: Where is this asked? As quick one mark questions: spot the base quantity, the derived one, or the vector.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Which set has only derived quantities that are also scalars? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is A. Speed, density and work.

A2.text: B has mass and time, both base. C has force, a vector.

A3.text: D has current and temperature, both base. Only A is fully derived and fully scalar.

Y2.text: One. Why is sugar, two, not a complete measurement?

Y3.text: Two. Why is speed a derived quantity?

Y4.text: Three. Is electric current a scalar or a vector, and why?
